# M365 Optimize Inspection Exemption — Decision Instruments {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning}
## These are templates, not completed records

All three carry bracketed fields requiring agency values, and Attachment A's
example rows use RFC 5737 documentation addresses. Nothing here is an
agency-approved form — confirm the structure against your own risk-acceptance
procedure and delegation of authority before use.
:::

## The problem these answer

A branch site running Microsoft 365 over local direct internet access has to
decide what happens to the **Optimize** endpoint set. Microsoft's connectivity
guidance says bypass inspection for it. The agency's boundary says inspect
everything. Both positions are defensible, and the gap between them is a
decision somebody has to sign.

These three instruments are the paperwork that decision needs. They exist
because the shape of the ask matters: this is not a generic risk acceptance but
a **documented traffic-flow exception under SC-7(4)**, which carries a specific
discipline — a named exception with its supporting mission need and duration,
reviewed on a stated cadence, with enforcement evidence that its boundaries
hold.

## The set

| Document | What it decides | Who signs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [SC-7(4) traffic-flow exception memo](sc7-4-exception-memo.qmd) | Whether to grant the exception, on named controls and stated compensating controls | Authorizing Official |
| [Attachment A — pilot site register](attachment-a-site-register.qmd) | Which sites and circuits are in scope, why each needs it, and when it ends | System owner, cited by the memo |
| [Attachment B — architecture review determination](attachment-b-architecture-review.qmd) | Whether the design is TIC 3.0 conformant and where each PEP capability now sits | Architecture review board |

**Keeping the memo and Attachment B separate is deliberate.** The architecture
review answers whether the design is conformant and where capabilities moved;
it does not accept risk. The Authorizing Official accepts the one thing that
cannot be transferred. Each signer answers a question that is actually theirs.

## What the set is careful about

**Naming the controls.** The exemption punctures SI-3, SI-4(10), AC-4 and AU-3
(with AU-12 by reference). Saying "inspection forgone" invites an assessor to
decide for themselves what was lost. **SC-8 is explicitly not a gap** —
Optimize flows carry TLS and SRTP, and the overlay encrypts the rest.

**Tenant restrictions.** Tenant-to-tenant exfiltration over an
Optimize-categorized path is the case an assessor will construct. The intuitive
answer — that tenant restrictions v2 needs an in-path proxy, so it is lost —
is wrong: that is the v1 model. Under v2 the Windows Group Policy path needs no
proxy and is the only one reaching the data plane. For a FedRAMP Moderate
agency it is also the *only* available path, since Global Secure Access is
non-FIPS in GCC Moderate. So the control moves to the endpoint rather than
disappearing — but only if it is configured and verified, which is why it is a
precondition to cutover in all three documents.

**The exception record.** SC-7(4) requires each exception documented with its
mission need and duration, and reviewed on a cadence. Attachment A's Table A1
carries those fields, because a register that lists circuits without recording
why each was granted an exception cannot evidence the control the memo claims.

**Policy Enforcement Parity.** The TIC 3.0 universal capability requiring
protections to apply *"independent of the communication mechanism, forwarding
path, or endpoints used"* is the one this design most strains against.
Attachment B records it rather than omitting it; the SC-7(4) exception is the
mechanism for documenting a bounded departure rather than denying there is one.
